title: The New Enterprise Battle Over Who Owns the Model
dek: Thinking Machines ships its first model — and it's the availability, not the benchmarks, that matters. Inkling is a base model built for fine-tuning, and it lands right as Microsoft trains its salesforce to attack the frontier labs on data trust. The new enterprise fight isn't which model you rent — it's who owns the one you customize.

oneIdea.headline: The next enterprise battle is over who owns the model you fine-tune.
oneIdea.summary: Thinking Machines released Inkling — a mediocre-on-benchmarks but strategically pointed open-weights model designed to be the base for its Tinker fine-tuning platform. It arrives the same week Microsoft trains its salesforce to argue that companies shouldn't trust OpenAI or Anthropic with their data. Two things converge: enterprises increasingly want cost control and data sovereignty, and multiple labs are racing to sell fine-tuning as the answer. Whether closed (Microsoft Frontier Tuning) or open (Inkling + Tinker), the question is no longer just which frontier model to rent — it's how much independence you want over the model itself. The bitter lesson may still win, but the experimental period is real and there's alpha for nimble teams.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: "Who owns the model you fine-tune" has an NHS translation: data sovereignty
items.body: The edition's core fight — rent a frontier model, or run and customise your own — lands squarely on the question every practice faces with an ambient scribe: where does the consultation data go, and who can train on it? An open-weights model you host, or a supplier who fine-tunes on your data but keeps it on your infrastructure, is the commercial version of what information governance already demands. If NLW's right, this competitive pressure gives buyers real leverage to insist on models that stay inside the data controller's walls. If Zitron's right, none of it is worth the spend regardless — so the safe move is unchanged: demand a clear data-processing agreement and confirm nothing leaves the practice unbidden, whoever's economics win.

items.title: Beware the 'fine-tuning is the answer' pitch in health IT
items.body: Two of the edition's own voices — Simon Smith and Zitron — warn that fine-tuning is far more effort and ongoing cost than vendors admit, needing constant curation as edge cases and model updates arrive. That caution matters for any practice or ICB tempted by a bespoke, 'trained-on-our-data' clinical tool. If Zitron's right, a big general model plus good prompting and local context often beats a hard-won custom model as token costs fall. If NLW's right, there's still real value for well-resourced teams — but general practice rarely has the data-engineering capacity to maintain a fine-tune, so the honest default is a well-governed general model, not a custom one you cannot keep current.

items.title: The Microsoft-attacks-rivals story is a reminder to judge tools on evidence, not sales scripts
items.body: Bloomberg's report that Microsoft is training salespeople to tell customers a rival model is "slower and less accurate" while sidestepping overall quality is a clean illustration of vendor incentive at work. In the surgery the parallel is exact: scribe and triage-tool claims should be checked against independent testing and your own audit, not the supplier's comparison slide. Whichever side of the bubble argument you take, the discipline is the same — measure accuracy and time saved on your own consultations before trusting anyone's marketing.

the_other_side.text: Zitron's case cuts underneath the whole model-ownership debate: to him it is a rounding error beside the fact that enterprise AI has no measurable return. He argues the boom rests not on ROI but on "vibes" and a "cult-like psychosis," and that no architectural choice — open weights, fine-tuning, closed tuning — changes the economics, because "without OpenAI, the AI industry doesn't exist." He notes API costs already "became a 'huge issue'" for enterprise customers, and that four years in there is still no agreed accounting of what these models actually cost to run. He would read Inkling and Microsoft Frontier Tuning not as sovereignty on offer but as fresh ways to keep spending on something that has not shown a return.

the_truth_beneath.text: The single variable both men orbit is enterprise AI economics — whether the cost of running these models is ever justified by the value enterprises get back. Both accept the same facts: token costs are large and real, and the unit economics are genuinely murky. The empirical question that will resolve is whether enterprises running fine-tuned or open-weights stacks show durable, auditable ROI; the observable that settles it is published enterprise unit economics and renewal data — does cost-per-outcome fall and does spend keep being renewed? The residue is pure worldview: NLW sees an experimental period with alpha for nimble teams, Zitron sees a capital misallocation heading for collapse. NLW is vindicated if fine-tuning lowers cost-per-outcome and enterprises keep paying and expanding; Zitron if spend keeps climbing while returns don't and a major player runs out of money. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom to an audience of buyers, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype to subscribers who reward it — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: enterprise token cost is a real, unsolved problem. Watch whether any enterprise publishes hard fine-tuning ROI numbers, or whether the bills just keep rising.

headlines.headline: Cursor wants to be a top-tier model developer, not just a coding tool
headlines.summary: The Information reported on a May all-hands where CEO Michael Truell said Cursor aims to produce a state-of-the-art model by year end and accrue a real compute advantage by 2027 — pushing the frontier itself, not staying limited to coding. SpaceX wanted Cursor for its brand, enterprise relationships, and go-to-market team.

headlines.headline: First SpaceX-Cursor model lands in Grok 4.5
headlines.summary: Setting aside recent data-retention controversy, the first SpaceX AI model trained in partnership with Cursor has been well received and is competitive. Cursor is also rumored to be building a competitor to Claude Cowork — its first big expansion beyond coding.

headlines.headline: SpaceX dips below its IPO price for the first time
headlines.summary: SpaceX traded down to $133 Wednesday, breaking the $135 IPO price before recovering to close at $135.27 — now down 33% from its all-time high, costing Musk his trillionaire status. Insider lockups don't start for another month.

headlines.headline: OpenAI leans toward a 2027 IPO; Anthropic pushes for fall
headlines.summary: Advisors reportedly told Altman a trillion-dollar market cap is unlikely, nudging OpenAI toward next year. Anthropic has appointed investment banks, added a couple billion in revolving credit, and is meeting investors — still targeting an IPO as early as September or October.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 Edge fills the physical-AI niche
headlines.summary: The new 4-billion-parameter open model is built to run on edge devices inside robots, functioning as both a world model and a vision-language model. It arrives alongside a fresh wave of robot designs and NVIDIA's expanded Toyota partnership across robots, smart cities, and factories.

headlines.headline: A new take on the family car: send it to run your errands
headlines.summary: A just-launched company called Chip combines AI and autonomy to turn a golf-cart-style vehicle into a robot — the launch video shows a dad sending it to fetch snacks at a soccer game or park itself after an Uber home. A herald of how AI integrates into the physical world.

headlines.headline: Apple is shopping to buy its way back into the AI race
headlines.summary: Per The Information, Apple is far along in an effort to acquire a chipmaker to build AI server chips, having spoken with bankers and approached semiconductor startups. Its own server-grade Baltra chip has been delayed, and it currently outsources to Google Cloud on NVIDIA hardware — a striking shift for a company whose biggest deal ever was $3B for Beats.

headlines.headline: The list of proven chip targets is painfully short
headlines.summary: NVIDIA just paid $20B for Groq, Cerebras is valued at $40B, and Broadcom's $1.8T valuation would make it a merger with huge antitrust exposure. Tenstorrent is a possible natural fit given ex-Apple designer Jim Keller — but no solid rumors yet.

headlines.headline: Microsoft trains its salesforce to attack OpenAI and Anthropic
headlines.summary: Per Bloomberg, Microsoft's new fiscal-year strategy has sales staff pushing MAI models' cost-effectiveness and its vertically integrated stack — telling customers Claude is "slower and less accurate" and lacks proper security integrations in Office, while sidestepping overall model quality.

headlines.headline: The pitch's subtext: don't trust OpenAI or Anthropic with your data
headlines.summary: NLW reads Microsoft's move as aligning with Nadella's argument that the frontier labs have an incentive to build competing services — and as a foot in the door for its own models before upselling customer-specific fine-tuning via Microsoft Frontier Tuning.

headlines.headline: Thinking Machines ships Inkling, its first LLM
headlines.summary: Mira Murati's lab released Inkling — a 975B-parameter MoE (41B active) with a 1M-token window that reasons natively across text, images, and audio — plus a 12B Inkling Small in preview. It's the first in a planned family and was pre-trained from scratch, aside from a small bootstrap distilled from Kimi K2.5.

headlines.headline: Inkling is not the strongest overall model available today, open or closed.
headlines.attribution: Thinking Machines Lab, Inkling launch post
headlines.summary: TML positioned Inkling honestly: a broad, balanced foundation model whose value is a combination of qualities — multimodal capabilities, efficient thinking, and availability on Tinker for fine-tuning — that make it a good open-weights base for customization.

headlines.headline: Competitive but not state-of-the-art — with strong token efficiency
headlines.summary: Inkling scores 29.7% on Humanity's Last Exam (46% with tools), 54.3% on SWE-Bench Pro, and 1238 on GDPVal — ahead of Nemotron and Kimi K2.5 but well behind GLM 5.2, 5.6 Sol, and Fable 5. Artificial Analysis ranked it 19th at 41, while noting it uses ~two-thirds the tokens per task of GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

headlines.headline: So far Inkling is pretty rough in my tests. Not close to frontier Chinese open weights models.
headlines.summary: Ethan Mollick reported it failed the LEM test that every frontier model has passed since DeepSeek-R1 and Sonnet 3.5, and that its chain of thought went haywire even on simple requests. First impressions were broadly unflattering.

headlines.headline: This is the only open weight model that's trained without distilling from OpenAI or Anthropic.
headlines.summary: Jack Morris argues Kimi, GLM, Qwen, and Nemotron all distill — making Inkling a fully different tech stack and the first pure open frontier coding model. A community note added TML did use a small bootstrap from open models like K2.5, and that Llama was also trained without lab distillation.

headlines.headline: Why "American and non-distilled" could suddenly matter to enterprises
headlines.summary: NLW's read: as enterprises pay more attention to open-weights models, the fact that Inkling is an American model not primarily distilled from a closed lab becomes meaningful — especially once lawyers and risk teams weigh in on data sovereignty.

headlines.headline: Inkling was somewhat inevitable once Tinker took off.
headlines.summary: Nathan Lambert frames Inkling as the integration of post-training services across TML's entire stack — "one of the best open model business stories to date." The model was designed to be the base model for the Tinker fine-tuning platform.

headlines.headline: Attack the labs' weakness: competitive paranoia over leaking alpha
headlines.summary: Jeffrey Emanuel argues open weights let companies run models on their own infrastructure without leaking data, and TML's clever answer to open-weights monetization is charging for fine-tuning a company's model on its own internal data — keeping the benefits exclusive to that company.

headlines.headline: Enter the forward-deployed fine-tuner.
headlines.summary: Daniel Kaplan sees a new services category: self-serve Inkling + Tinker for teams with AI researchers, plus a high-priced forward-deployed fine-tuner for those without — scaling to big companies, AI startups protecting their alpha, and app-layer companies chasing cheaper tokens.

headlines.headline: Microsoft's fine-tuning still requires trusting Microsoft
headlines.summary: NLW notes Microsoft Frontier Tuning on MAI models rides on decades of built-up enterprise trust — an easier leap than trusting OpenAI or Anthropic — but it still looks very different from an open-weights option like Inkling that offers real independence and sovereignty.

headlines.headline: Thinking Machines is basically a bet against the bitter lesson.
headlines.summary: Simon Smith is unconvinced: fine-tuning is far more effort than people think, ongoing to handle edge cases and model updates, and a big general model plus a bit of context often beats hard-won fine-tunes as token costs collapse. Teams frequently ignore the fully loaded cost of curating data and maintaining pipelines.

headlines.headline: Recognizing the problem doesn't mean today's answers are right
headlines.summary: NLW cautions that acknowledging real challenges in data sovereignty and token cost doesn't mean Microsoft Frontier Tuning or Tinker is the ultimate solution. The flip side: as an open-weights model, Inkling addresses both the cost and sovereignty sides at once, whereas a closed fine-tuning solution may be caught in between.

headlines.headline: Organizations are trading frontier access for control over their data
headlines.attribution: Sriram Krishnan, former White House AI advisor and a16z investor
headlines.summary: Sriram Krishnan lists the forces behind open source's moment: you can now catch near-SOTA with clean lineage; many well-funded teams exist; organizations fear enabling a future competitor; open source is a slider you tune; companies now worry about ballooning token costs; and countries want frontier tokens inside controlled environments.

headlines.headline: Enterprises' choice has exploded far beyond "OpenAI or Anthropic"
headlines.summary: NLW argues the decision now spans models, the harnesses they live in, and complex multi-model architectures including fine-tuning approaches. Not every flower will bloom, and the juggernauts may absorb the best ideas — but the experimental period will shape the eventual solutions, with real alpha for nimble teams.

headlines.headline: You don't have to sign up — but you can't ignore this
headlines.summary: NLW's bottom line for buyers: no need to rush into Tinker or Microsoft Frontier Tuning or switch everything to OpenRouter, but if you make enterprise buying decisions and aren't at least experimenting with or closely watching these fine-tuning and open-weights options, you're missing real opportunity.
